## Do derivatives always reach zero? {#gac2-always-zero .gac-lesson}

<p class="eyebrow">Additional question · Think, then discuss</p>
<p class="gac-lead">Our cubic eventually differentiated to zero.<br>Will this happen to every function?</p>
<p class="gac-prompt"><strong>What makes you say that?</strong></p>

<div data-module="reveal-panel" class="gac2-counterexample">
<button class="toggle-panel" aria-pressed="false" aria-controls="gac2-counterexample-answer">Show</button>
<div id="gac2-counterexample-answer" class="panel-answer" hidden>
<p>Consider <span data-math="f(x)=e^x"></span>.</p>
<p data-math="f'(x)=e^x,\qquad f''(x)=e^x,\qquad f^{(n)}(x)=e^x"></p>
<p>Every derivative is the same non-zero function.</p>
</div>
</div>

::: notes
2 minutes. Exact student prompt: "Our cubic eventually differentiated to zero. Will this happen to every function? What makes you say that?" Give individual thinking time, then a brief paired explanation before collecting reasons.

Purpose: distinguish a pattern for polynomials from a universal claim about functions. Use the familiar exponential derivative as a counterexample. Reveal it only after students have had a chance to supply one; the button can hide it again. The n-th derivative statement is for positive integers n. e^x is positive for every real x.

A polynomial of degree m has constant m-th derivative and identically zero derivatives of every order greater than m. This does not mean that a single zero value of one derivative makes all higher derivatives zero. Students may offer sine or cosine as other counterexamples.

Project Zero, Harvard Graduate School of Education, What Makes You Say That? (adapted): https://www.pz.harvard.edu/resources/what-makes-you-say . Ask for mathematical evidence rather than accepting a prediction alone.
:::
